name: carbon dioxide
why: The two C=O dipoles point in exactly opposite directions along a straight line, so they cancel completely.

name: carbon disulfide
why: Linear and symmetric — the two identical bond dipoles cancel.

name: hydrogen cyanide
why: Linear, but the two ends are DIFFERENT (H on one side, N on the other), so there is nothing to cancel against. Linear does not automatically mean nonpolar.

name: boron trifluoride
why: Three identical dipoles at 120° in a plane sum to zero — the same reason three equal forces at 120° balance.

name: methane
why: C–H bonds are barely polar to begin with, and the tetrahedral arrangement is perfectly symmetric, so there is no net dipole.

name: carbon tetrachloride
why: Four strongly polar C–Cl bonds, but they point to the corners of a tetrahedron and cancel exactly. This is the classic 'polar bonds, nonpolar molecule' case.

name: chloroform
why: Tetrahedral, but one corner holds an H instead of a Cl. That breaks the symmetry, so the three C–Cl dipoles no longer cancel.

name: dichloromethane
why: Two Cl and two H on a tetrahedron is not symmetric, so the dipoles add to a net dipole pointing toward the chlorines.

name: chloromethane
why: One polar C–Cl bond and three nearly nonpolar C–H bonds — nothing cancels it.

name: water
why: The two O–H dipoles point down-and-outward from a bent geometry, so they add rather than cancel. The lone pairs push the molecule out of linearity.

name: hydrogen sulfide
why: Bent like water, so the bond dipoles cannot cancel — though S–H is much less polar than O–H.

name: sulfur dioxide
why: A lone pair on sulfur bends the molecule, so the two S=O dipoles add instead of cancelling. Compare CO₂, which is linear and cancels.

name: ammonia
why: The lone pair makes it pyramidal rather than planar, so the three N–H dipoles sum to a net dipole pointing up through the lone pair.

name: phosphorus trichloride
why: Pyramidal because of the lone pair, so the dipoles do not cancel. Contrast BF₃, which is planar and does cancel.

name: hydrogen chloride
why: A single polar bond has nothing to cancel against, so every diatomic with two different atoms is polar.

name: oxygen
why: Two identical atoms share the electrons equally, so there is no bond dipole at all.

name: methanol
why: The polar O–H and C–O bonds sit in an asymmetric arrangement — this is why methanol mixes with water.

name: benzene
why: A perfectly symmetric ring of nearly nonpolar C–H bonds. Benzene is a standard nonpolar solvent.

name: ethene
why: Symmetric and built from nearly nonpolar C–H bonds, so there is no net dipole.

name: sulfur hexafluoride
why: Six very polar S–F bonds arranged octahedrally cancel in every direction — polar bonds, perfectly nonpolar molecule.
